newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany asks: is there an SPD Blair to beat Kohl?.
newsitem.headline: Germany asks: is there an SPD Blair to beat Kohl?.

text.p: Germany asked on Sunday whether the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) can find their own Tony Blair to pose a real challenge to Chancellor Helmut Kohl at the 1998 elections and mirror the victory of Britain's Labour Party.

"If only there was a German Blair...," mused a headline in the news weekly Der Spiegel, its cover depicting the two main SPD hopefuls -- party leader Oskar Lafontaine and the maverick Gerhard Schroeder gazing longingly up at a beaming Blair.

"The overwhelming election victory has given the German SPD new courage: the Bonn coalition no longer looks unbeatable. But the SPD still doesn't want to go ahead with the most important step -- deciding on its chancellor candidate," wrote Spiegel, in an advance copy ahead of publication on Monday.

Commentators said Schroeder, the media-friendly and pro-business premier of Lower Saxony, was the closest thing Germany had to Britain's Blair, who led his newly-modernised Labour party to election victory on Friday.
"Schroeder... is credited with having the most Blair-like role in the SPD," wrote the Welt am Sonntag Sunday paper.

But commentators say, in contrast to Blair, Schroeder is an outsider in the SPD and could only run against Kohl with the agreement of SPD leader Lafontaine, who also has his sights on the top job despite losing to Kohl in 1990.
The SDP has said it will not chose its candidate until its party congress in April next year, although Kohl announced he would stand for a fifth term last month.

Schroeder, who opinion polls say has a far better chance of ending 14 years of opposition for the SDP than Lafontaine, made Blair-like overtures at the weekend in interviews during a tour of the United States to meet business leaders.

"The SPD wants to win, therefore it will understand that we have to change ourselves," Schroeder told Focus magazine in an interview released ahead of publication on Monday. "Otherwise the danger is great we will be written off as old-fashioned."

Schroeder, often photographed smoking a fat cigar, called on his party to reach out to those it had once labelled as the better-off and said Germany had to consider how much of the welfare state was still affordable. "This will hurt many of us, but the SPD must also carry out this process," he said.
Lafontaine, in contrast, is seen as closer to the left, less keen to move away from the German model of social democracy and is his party's favourite to challenge Kohl.

The Welt am Sonntag noted that the last SPD politician to drawn lessons from a foreign election campaign was a young Willy Brandt who led an U.S.-style election campaign in 1961 after John F. Kennedy was elected U.S. President in 1960.

"Although it wasn't quite enough for victory... he (Brandt) tore social democracy out of its lethargy," it wrote. "If the SPD wants to imitate its sister party (Labour), it needs a young, beaming man with charisma and the power to convince."
But several commentators noted that both Lafontaine and Schroeder, both 53, were much older than the 43-year-old Blair.

German-born British sociologist Lord Ralf Dahrendorf warned the SPD against being too eager to follow Blair's example. "It would be a mistake if the SPD thought Blair would be its life saver and it could copy his recipe for electoral success," he said.
But Dahrendorf, who sits in the British upper house of parliament, told Spiegel the SPD should learn not to let its opponents dictate the agenda of an election campaign.
But master election strategist Kohl has already made his first move, wrong-footing the SPD by choosing to announce his candidacy early.

Heide Simonis, SPD premier of Schleswig Holstein, told Bild am Sonntag the party should have left open when to choose a candidate, rather than binding itself to next April after elections in Schroeder's state of Lower Saxony.
"The right moment for the naming of the SPD chancellor candidate could be earlier than spring 1998," she said.
But the general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) Peter Hintze said he expects Lafontaine to be the SPD candidate.

"Schroeder will unceremoniously be moved out of the running after the Lower Saxony state parliament elections. Then there will only be Lafontaine left," Hintze told Saturday's Magdeburger Volksstimme daily.
